This phrase appears as the epigraph or chapter heading at the opening of the chapter. It serves as a thematic introduction to the events that follow—namely, the preparations for and anticipation of Edith's wedding to Captain Lennox. The phrase encapsulates the romantic narrative arc that drives the chapter's action, from the discussion of wedding arrangements and trousseau to the arrival of the bridegroom himself on the evening of the farewell dinner party.
c1:p1: Margaret gently tries to wake her cousin Edith, who has fallen asleep on the sofa in the back drawing-room during a conversation about wedding preparations and Edith's upcoming marriage to Captain Lennox.
c1:p2: This passage opens the chapter and establishes the domestic scene at Mrs. Shaw's house in Harley Street, London. Margaret finds her cousin Edith asleep on the sofa after they have been discussing wedding preparations and Edith's impending marriage to Captain Lennox. The narrator reflects on Margaret's newfound appreciation of Edith's beauty as she contemplates their imminent separation, as Margaret will soon return to live with her parents at the country parsonage in Helstone while Edith moves to Corfu as a soldier's wife.
c1:p3: Margaret discovers that Edith has fallen asleep on the sofa during the farewell dinner party. Unable to share her thoughts about her impending move to Helstone parsonage with her cousin, Margaret overhears her aunt Shaw discussing Edith's upcoming marriage to Captain Lennox with the dinner guests, while reflecting on her own mixed emotions about leaving London for her father's country parish.

c2:p0: This epigraph appears at the opening of the chapter and sets the pastoral, nostalgic tone for Margaret Hale's return to her childhood home at Helstone parsonage after years away in London. It establishes the financial constraints of the Hale family, Mrs. Hale's discontent with their modest circumstances, and the contrast between Mrs. Shaw's comfortable life and the Hales' limited means. The scene sets up Margaret's transition from her social life in Harley Street to rural parish life, while hinting at underlying domestic tensions that will develop throughout the chapter.
c2:p2: This passage occurs at the beginning of Margaret Hale's journey home to Helstone after attending her cousin's wedding in London. Exhausted from her busy social duties in Harley Street, Margaret reflects on leaving behind her London life while traveling by railway with her father. c2:p5: Margaret returns to her childhood home at Helstone parsonage in late July after attending her cousin's wedding in London. During the visit, tension arose when Margaret Hale made a comment about Mrs. Thornton's attachment to Milton, and Mrs. Thornton responded defensively by promoting the town's manufacturing importance—a topic in which Margaret showed little interest. This moment reveals Mrs. Thornton's critical judgment of the Hale family and her protective attitude toward her daughter's social connections.
